title: The end of video games is nigh (apparently)
author: Christopher Dring

The end of video games is nigh (apparently)
Here’s The Dring: Tackling growing industry anxiety on the eve of the biggest game launch ever
Christopher Dring
Nov 16 ∙ Paid
Every Monday we do a bonus podcast/newsletter for paid supporters of The Game Business (called Here’s The Dring). This is that edition! If you like The Game Business, why not consider becoming a paid supporter? An annual sub works out at about $2/£1.53 a week. It also supports all our free episodes we do every Tuesday and Thursday.
Hello there!
This week is the week. After numerous delays, rumours and drama, GTA 6 finally arrives on PlayStation and Xbox. Is it the industry saviour? Probably not. But I’m not entirely convinced it needs one.
This week, I am tackling growing industry fears about its future. And I briefly touch on Sony’s continued pivot away from live service. Plus, the industry gets angry over EU’s Digital Fairness Act.
Enjoy!
Our Rami Ismail interview last week ran longer than we could fit into a single episode. So, I am going to share a few quotes from the indie games veteran that didn’t make the cut.
“There are no B2C indies left, there’s like a few dozen of them,” he told me. “Most indies are B2B at the moment. We all have to make games to sell to publishers. We’re not building for the audience, we’re building for a pitch. And when we get the pitch, then we build for an audience, but then it’s no longer B2C because we’re working for another company.
“We are in this weird rat race where the Tim Sweeneys and the Gabe Newells and the Asha Sharmas and the Hermen Hulsts, all these interests that control these platforms, all have really good reason to not be betting on us.
“[They have good reasons] to just let us do our thing, and if [their platforms] harm us, it doesn’t matter because it just means somebody else wins. As long as they’re the 30% in the middle of this, they don’t care. But if they’re looking at how to spend that 30%, it’s much better spent on maybe winning the AI wars than it is spent on supporting game development.
“To me, this algorithmic rat race that we’re all in, where we’re all just clawing at each other, is a nightmare scenario. Because to me, independent game development has always felt like this very communal thing. And now it’s not together anymore. We’re all just individually fighting the algorithm.”
His concerns are the platforms are simply too dominant, and that AI will make it worse: “Now we’re also funnelling creation through a number of platforms owned by a very few people.”
That’s a bit that didn’t make the episode, but the stuff that did was similar in tone. We talked about AI cloning, the collapse of Steam Next Fest and risk averse publishers.
Ismail’s concerns are not unreasonable. Game developers are beholden to the policies, practices, strategies and algorithms built by just a few large organizations. Publishers aren’t rolling the dice on new ideas, and AI chancers are stealing people’s ideas.
And that’s just some of a myriad of anxieties that are being felt by companies, of all sizes, that are operating in video games today. This week we’ve got an interview with Ben Feder, the former Take-Two CEO turned VC, who talks candidly about the disruption in the market. He believes the rise of AI-driven video game recompilations could be as disruptive to games as Napster was for music. And he has a pessimistic view on the future of AAA games.
“They’re not big enough to really be platforms, and they’re not small enough to really innovate,” he told us. “If you talk to the major publishers, they cannot figure out a way to make a game for less than $300 million. That to me is just not sustainable.”
Then there are the legislatives fears. The reaction to the draft EU Digital Fairness Act is akin to a full-blown panic. Every major European trade body has issued statements and CEOs have descended upon LinkedIn to have their say.
Discoverability and funding remain major challenges, and companies are cutting and cutting and cutting. Just this week, Skydance, Tripwire Interactive and Bit Reactor have all laid off employees. Bandai Namco has closed its Reflector Entertainment studio, while mobile games companies Fortis Games and Playnest has shut its doors. Meanwhile, PlayStation has cancelled two in-development live service games.
Analysts are predicting the demise of Switch 2 following Nintendo’s latest financial report. And the hope that GTA 6 will reinvigorate the market have turned into doubts. Circana games boss Mat Piscatella noted how the average price of consoles today is $300 higher (even when accounting for inflation) than they were when GTA 5 came out. He expects to see some increase in console sales, but is warning us against getting our hopes too high.
The cost of Gears of War, the end of BioWare, component price rises, Xbox redundancies, the death of discs, the flood of AI Steam games, the collapse of Western game studios… it all seems dire. The end of video games is nigh.
I’m aware of the wider media trend of leaning into this anxiety. So many of the podcasts I listen to seem full of AI ‘experts’ predicting some form of cataclysm. And people are tuning in. We’ve become a society of apocaholics.
And it’s not that the concerns aren’t valid or real. In games, we know there is real disruption, confusion and pain. According to GDC’s latest industry survey, 54% of those who had been laid off have not found new employment. Things aren’t ok.
But please indulge me as I try to bring a bit of sunlight to the gloom.
